title: Metabolic Alkalosis: Chloride, Volume, Potassium, Cause
bottomLine: Metabolic alkalosis reflects bicarbonate gain/retention or hydrogen/chloride loss. The practical split is often chloride/volume-responsive versus persistent mineralocorticoid/renal causes; potassium depletion both results from and sustains the disorder.
recognize: Vomiting/NG suction and diuretics commonly produce chloride depletion and volume contraction.
Severe alkalemia can worsen arrhythmia, reduce ionized calcium and impair oxygen delivery, especially when hypokalemia is present.
differentiate: Compensatory hypoventilation is limited; marked CO2 elevation beyond expected compensation suggests an added respiratory acidosis.
Persistent hypertension with alkalosis/hypokalemia raises mineralocorticoid excess rather than simple GI loss.
assessment: Assess vomiting/NG losses, diuretics, volume status, BP, potassium/chloride, laxative/antacid use, endocrine clues and respiratory reserve.
workup: Use electrolytes, blood gas and urine chloride when clinically helpful to distinguish ongoing renal chloride loss/mineralocorticoid physiology from chloride depletion.
management: Correct the cause, volume/chloride and potassium when appropriate; stop unnecessary losses/diuretics and treat mineralocorticoid disorders specifically.
medicationSafety: Aggressive potassium replacement requires renal/ECG context; acetazolamide or acidifying strategies are selected acute-care tools, not routine first-line therapy for every alkalosis.
counselling: Review diuretic/laxative/antacid use and the reason potassium/chloride replacement may be part of treatment.
followUp: Trend electrolytes and bicarbonate after cause-directed therapy; persistent unexplained alkalosis requires renal/endocrine evaluation.
examTrap: Giving repeated potassium while ongoing vomiting/diuretic chloride loss continues—or missing mineralocorticoid excess in a hypertensive hypokalemic patient.
oneLinePearl: Metabolic alkalosis usually asks two questions first: where did chloride go and why is potassium low?

title: Mixed Acid-Base Disorders: When Compensation Does Not Fit
bottomLine: A near-normal pH can hide two serious opposing acid-base disorders. Identify the primary process, test whether compensation is physiologically appropriate, calculate anion gap when indicated and let the clinical syndrome explain the combination.
recognize: DKA plus vomiting can produce high-gap acidosis and metabolic alkalosis; sepsis/salicylates can produce metabolic acidosis plus respiratory alkalosis; COPD plus diuresis can combine respiratory acidosis with metabolic alkalosis.
Compensation moves in a predictable direction but does not fully normalize the pH; values outside the expected range suggest a second primary disorder.
differentiate: Do not label every abnormal CO2 as a primary respiratory disorder; determine whether it is compensation first.
A normal pH is not proof of normal acid-base physiology.
assessment: Assess the entire syndrome—ventilation, shock/sepsis, diabetes/ketones, vomiting/diuretics, renal failure and toxins.
workup: Use pH, PaCO2, bicarbonate, electrolytes/anion gap and cause-specific lactate/ketones/toxicology; compare observed compensation with expected physiology.
management: Treat each underlying cause rather than chasing pH; mixed respiratory failure plus metabolic acidosis often represents a higher-risk patient because compensation is failing.
medicationSafety: Bicarbonate, ventilator changes, insulin and electrolyte replacement can each shift the acid-base picture; reassess after major interventions.
redFlags: DKA with vomiting or renal failure
Rapidly changing gas after ventilation change
counselling: After recovery, explain the underlying disease processes rather than teaching the patient to interpret arterial gases independently.
followUp: Repeat gases only when clinical trajectory/intervention makes the result actionable.
examTrap: Seeing pH 7.40 and declaring the acid-base status normal despite a low bicarbonate and low CO2 from two simultaneous processes.
oneLinePearl: Normal pH can be the midpoint of two dangerous disorders pulling in opposite directions.

title: Sepsis Lab Recognition: Organ Dysfunction Beats One Biomarker
system: Lab Interpretation / Infectious Disease / Critical Care
bottomLine: No laboratory test diagnoses sepsis alone. The dangerous pattern is suspected infection plus new organ dysfunction—lactate/perfusion abnormality, AKI, thrombocytopenia/coagulopathy, hypoxemia, hepatic dysfunction or altered mental status—combined with the bedside trajectory.
recognize: High or low WBC, rising creatinine, falling platelets, lactate elevation and metabolic acidosis can support severity but are not specific.
Older/immunocompromised patients may have severe infection without fever or leukocytosis.
differentiate: Lactate can rise from nonseptic shock, seizures, adrenergic states or impaired clearance; procalcitonin/CRP cannot independently rule sepsis in or out.
A positive culture without a compatible syndrome may represent colonization/contamination rather than sepsis.
assessment: Assess ABCs, perfusion, mental status, oxygenation, urine output, source, immune status and goals of care while labs are pending.
workup: Obtain cultures/source-directed studies when feasible without delaying treatment; use CBC, renal/electrolytes, lactate and coagulation/organ tests based on severity.
management: Begin time-sensitive resuscitation, empiric antimicrobials and source-control planning when sepsis/shock is clinically likely; reassess after each intervention.
medicationSafety: Avoid nephrotoxic/renally inappropriate regimens without adjustment and avoid fixed fluid assumptions when HF/renal disease or poor fluid responsiveness is present.
counselling: After stabilization, explain that sepsis was recognized from the whole physiologic pattern, not one blood test.
followUp: Close the loop on cultures, antibiotic narrowing/duration, source control and post-sepsis organ/function recovery.
examTrap: Waiting for a positive culture, procalcitonin or WBC elevation before treating infection with clear new organ dysfunction.
oneLinePearl: Sepsis labs support the story; organ dysfunction and trajectory define the danger.
sourceBasis: Canadian acute-care sepsis and antimicrobial stewardship practice principles

title: DKA Lab Patterns: Ketones and Acidosis Must Resolve
bottomLine: DKA is a ketosis/acidosis emergency, not simply high glucose. Follow beta-hydroxybutyrate/ketones, bicarbonate/pH, anion gap where used, potassium, renal function and clinical perfusion; glucose can normalize before ketoacidosis resolves and SGLT2-associated DKA may occur without marked hyperglycemia.
recognize: Ketosis plus metabolic acidosis supports DKA; dehydration and total-body potassium depletion are typical even when serum potassium begins normal/high.
Euglycemic DKA must be considered with SGLT2 inhibitors, fasting/pregnancy or insulin deficiency when symptoms/ketosis fit.
differentiate: Starvation/alcoholic ketosis and lactic acidosis can overlap; HHS has hyperosmolar dehydration with less prominent ketoacidosis.
assessment: Assess mental status, perfusion, vomiting/abdominal pain, infection/MI triggers, insulin access/omission, pump failure, pregnancy and SGLT2 use.
workup: Use glucose, electrolytes/renal function, beta-hydroxybutyrate/ketones and venous/arterial acid-base data; calculate osmolality/HHS context and investigate the precipitant.
management: Use protocolized fluids, potassium-aware insulin and dextrose when needed to continue clearing ketones; treat the cause and continue until ketoacidosis resolves clinically/biochemically.
medicationSafety: Insulin can rapidly worsen hypokalemia; do not start blindly in severe potassium depletion. Hold SGLT2 inhibitors during DKA/acute severe illness and use current sick-day/perioperative guidance.
counselling: Teach sick-day ketone testing, insulin continuity/pump-failure backup and when vomiting/ketones require urgent care.
followUp: Before discharge, correct the precipitant and medication/access problem that allowed DKA to occur.
examTrap: Stopping the insulin protocol because glucose normalized while ketones/acidosis remain.
oneLinePearl: In DKA, the endpoint is resolution of ketoacidosis—not merely a normal glucose.

title: GI Bleed Lab Trends: Hemodynamics First, Hemoglobin Second
bottomLine: Acute GI hemorrhage is a perfusion problem before it is a hemoglobin number. Early hemoglobin may underestimate blood loss before fluid equilibration; use hemodynamics, ongoing bleeding, serial CBC, renal/urea context, anticoagulation and response to resuscitation to judge severity.
recognize: Melena/hematemesis/hematochezia plus tachycardia, orthostasis, hypotension, syncope or poor perfusion raises urgency regardless of the first hemoglobin.
Hemoglobin can fall after crystalloid/equilibration even when visible bleeding has slowed; trend must be interpreted with fluid and clinical course.
differentiate: FOBT/FIT is a screening tool in asymptomatic populations, not a diagnostic test for overt/suspected acute GI bleeding.
High urea relative to creatinine may support upper GI bleeding but is not diagnostic.
assessment: Assess ABCs, perfusion, bleeding amount/tempo, anticoagulants/antiplatelets/NSAIDs, liver disease/varices, pregnancy and comorbidity.
workup: Use serial CBC, renal/electrolytes, coagulation/drug timing and type/crossmatch as severity warrants; arrange endoscopic/CT angiographic evaluation through the acute GI-bleed pathway.
management: Resuscitate and obtain urgent endoscopic/specialty care for instability/ongoing significant bleeding; use blood products based on clinical status and evidence-based restrictive strategies in stable nonmassive bleeding rather than one universal number.
medicationSafety: Review anticoagulant reversal when major bleeding warrants it; do not use FOBT to decide whether obvious bleeding is real.
counselling: After stabilization, review NSAID/anticoagulant safety and the cause-specific recurrence plan.
followUp: Close pending endoscopy/pathology/medication changes and ensure anemia/iron deficiency is corrected when appropriate.
examTrap: Reassuring a hypotensive patient because the first hemoglobin is normal—or ordering FOBT for visible melena.
oneLinePearl: In acute hemorrhage, vital signs can become abnormal before hemoglobin does.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada Gastroenterology/Clinical Biochemistry recommendations
Choosing Wisely Canada Transfusion Medicine recommendations

title: Heart Failure Lab Patterns: Congestion, Kidney, Electrolytes, Cause
bottomLine: Heart-failure labs support congestion severity, precipitant and medication safety but do not replace examination/echo. Interpret BNP/NT-proBNP with renal function, age/rhythm/body habitus, and trend creatinine, sodium and potassium as you decongest and optimize disease-modifying therapy.
recognize: Natriuretic peptides support HF probability/risk when interpreted in context; renal dysfunction can elevate them independently.
Hyponatremia, worsening renal function and hepatic congestion can mark advanced decompensation but also shift during treatment.
differentiate: A creatinine rise during effective decongestion is not automatically a reason to stop all HF therapy; assess perfusion, volume and trajectory.
BNP elevation is not specific to one EF phenotype or to volume overload alone.
assessment: Assess JVP/edema/lungs/weight, perfusion/BP, rhythm/ischemia, medication adherence, NSAIDs, infection and renal baseline.
workup: Use CBC, electrolytes/renal function, glucose, troponin when indicated, natriuretic peptide and echocardiography/cause-directed testing according to presentation.
management: Treat congestion/precipitant and titrate guideline therapy with renal/potassium/BP surveillance; escalate pulmonary edema, shock, severe AKI/electrolyte instability or ischemia.
medicationSafety: RAAS/ARNI/MRA therapy needs potassium/renal monitoring; diuretics can produce sodium/potassium/magnesium abnormalities; SGLT2 inhibitors need sick-day safety.
counselling: Teach weight/symptom monitoring and medication/lab follow-up without telling patients to self-adjust multiple drugs from one lab value unless they have an explicit plan.
followUp: Reassess renal/electrolytes after meaningful HF medication/diuretic changes and confirm decongestion plus chronic-treatment plan.
examTrap: Stopping beneficial HF therapy reflexively for a small creatinine rise without reassessing volume/perfusion—or diagnosing HF from BNP alone.
oneLinePearl: Heart-failure labs only make sense beside the volume and perfusion exam.
sourceBasis: Canadian Cardiovascular Society Heart Failure guidance

title: Shock Lab Patterns: Perfusion Failure Is a Trend
bottomLine: Shock is inadequate tissue perfusion, not a lactate diagnosis. Use hemodynamics, mental status, skin/urine output, acid-base/lactate, renal/liver injury, hemoglobin and bedside cause clues together; a normalized blood pressure with worsening lactate/oliguria can still be unresolved shock.
recognize: Rising lactate/metabolic acidosis, AKI/oliguria, hepatic injury and altered mentation can indicate ongoing hypoperfusion.
Different shock types produce different bedside/lab patterns and require different treatment—hemorrhage, sepsis, cardiogenic and obstructive shock cannot be managed by identical fluid recipes.
differentiate: Lactate can rise without shock and can remain elevated after perfusion improves; trend and context matter.
A normal BP does not exclude compensated shock, especially early hemorrhage or in younger patients.
assessment: Assess airway/breathing, pulse/BP, capillary refill/skin, mental status, urine output, bleeding, infection, cardiac/PE/tamponade/tension-pneumothorax clues and pregnancy.
workup: Use CBC, electrolytes/renal/liver, lactate/gas, troponin/ECG, cultures, bedside ultrasound and cause-specific imaging according to the suspected shock type.
management: Treat cause and perfusion simultaneously: hemorrhage control/blood, antibiotics/source control, cardiac support/reperfusion, obstruction relief, appropriate fluids/vasopressors with frequent reassessment.
medicationSafety: Fixed large-volume fluid strategies can harm cardiogenic/renal-failure patients; vasopressors and transfusion require monitored, cause-specific use.
counselling: After recovery, explain the precipitating cause and medication/follow-up changes rather than focusing on the highest lactate value.
followUp: Track organ recovery and unresolved cause; persistent AKI/cardiac injury/post-sepsis symptoms require follow-up.
examTrap: Declaring shock resolved because BP normalized after fluids while urine output worsens and lactate continues to rise.
oneLinePearl: Perfusion is a bedside-and-trend diagnosis; one pressure or lactate cannot certify recovery.

title: Multi-Lab Clinical Judgment: Which Pattern Changes the Next Action?
bottomLine: Real patients rarely present with one isolated lab. Prioritize the cluster that threatens airway, breathing, circulation, neurologic status or irreversible organ injury; then decide which abnormality is cause, consequence, compensation or treatment effect before acting.
recognize: Dangerous clusters include hyperkalemia plus ECG change/AKI; falling hemoglobin plus hypotension/bleeding; DKA ketosis/acidosis plus potassium shift; sepsis organ dysfunction plus perfusion failure; HF congestion plus renal/electrolyte change.
A dramatic but chronic stable abnormality can be less urgent than a modest new change paired with instability.
differentiate: Correlation is not causation: multiple abnormalities may arise from one underlying process or from treatment.
Reference-range severity and clinical priority are different concepts; the most abnormal number is not always the first problem.
assessment: Start with patient stability, symptoms, trend/timing, medications/interventions, baseline disease and which result changed most recently.
workup: Select follow-up tests that discriminate the leading dangerous mechanisms and avoid shotgun repetition of every abnormal panel.
management: Stabilize the physiologic threat, treat the cause, reassess response and document ownership of pending/critical results; de-escalate testing once it no longer changes care.
medicationSafety: Many interventions change labs quickly—insulin/potassium, diuretics/electrolytes, fluids/hemoglobin, anticoagulants/coagulation—so post-treatment interpretation must account for what was just given.
redFlags: Any lab cluster with hemodynamic/neurologic/respiratory instability
counselling: For stable chronic disease, translate the pattern into a small number of actionable patient goals rather than overwhelming the patient with every abnormal value.
followUp: Assign ownership for all pending tests and document what result triggers escalation, medication change or repeat assessment.
examTrap: Choosing the numerically most abnormal result instead of the pattern that indicates immediate physiologic danger.
oneLinePearl: Clinical judgment is deciding which lab pattern changes what you do next.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada laboratory stewardship principles
